findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Bind the supersedes proof to a store-identity anchor that a pre-epoch store can still verify (e.g. the pre-swap root commit sha(s) or the replaced remote tip recorded in the superseding record and checked against local HEAD), or require S2 to stamp a unique epoch with a normal fast-forward before any swap and refuse the override when the local epoch is null.
evidence: Plan: 'That lineage is the proof that the remote is a rewrite of THIS store, not an unrelated store, so unrelated stores keep today's refusal.'

compat.remote_epoch_supersedes_local returns `lineage is not None and local_epoch in lineage`; with no local record, local_epoch is None (compat.py:161-168, 274-288), so any remote lineage containing null passes.
compat.superseding_record appends `old_epoch` (None for a pre-epoch record) to the lineage (compat.py:297-307), so every first reclaim yields [null].
findings.finding: The epoch_lineage 'proof' does not prove that the remote rewrote THIS store when the local epoch is absent (null). Every store today is pre-epoch, so the first reclaim of any store stamps lineage [null]. Any local pre-epoch store with ticket events would then accept ANY first-generation reclaimed remote as its successor and be reset --hard onto it, including an unrelated project's store reached through a misconfigured or reused remote. This contradicts the plan's claim that 'unrelated stores keep today's refusal'.
findings.location: Approach — 'A reclaimed baseline is identified by … epoch_lineage list names the local epoch (JSON null stands for the pre-epoch/absent record). That lineage is the proof that the remote is a rewrite of THIS store'
scenarios: A pre-epoch clone whose sync.remote is pointed at a different project's tickets branch after that project ran its first reclaim: today it refuses with DIVERGED; under this plan it is hard-reset onto the foreign store, and if 'stale' its unpushed events are discarded.
Two unrelated stores, both reclaimed for the first time, both carry lineage [null]; neither proves anything about the other.
findings.suggested_fix: Have superseding_record also record the superseded history's root commit(s) (`git rev-list --max-parents=0 <old tip>`), e.g. as `superseded_roots`. Have remote_epoch_supersedes_local additionally require that local HEAD's root commit(s) appear in that list, so a null/absent local epoch can only match a rewrite of its own history. Add a test: a pre-epoch local store against an unrelated remote with lineage [null] must still refuse with DIVERGED.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the lineage proof sound for pre-epoch clones: either require an additional store-identity check (e.g. a root/first-commit or store-id match) when the local epoch is absent, or refuse with DIVERGED when the only lineage match is `null`; add a test with an unrelated `[null]`-lineage remote.
evidence: "JSON `null` stands for the pre-epoch/absent record"
"That lineage is the proof that the remote is a rewrite of THIS store, not an unrelated store, so unrelated stores keep today's refusal."
The unrelated-remote test only covers 'different epoch, lineage not naming the local epoch'. There is no case where the local epoch is absent and the unrelated remote's lineage contains null.
findings.finding: The lineage proof is not unique when the local store is pre-epoch. JSON `null` is used for every absent record, so ANY store's first reclaim produces a lineage of `[null]`. A pre-epoch clone pointed at an unrelated store that has been reclaimed once would therefore pass `remote_epoch_supersedes_local` and be hard-reset onto the unrelated store. This contradicts the Approach's claim that lineage proves 'the remote is a rewrite of THIS store, not an unrelated store'.
findings.location: Approach ¶1 (epoch_lineage / null sentinel); Testing 'Failure/edge' bullet
scenarios: A clone that never received an epoch record has its remote URL repointed (or misconfigured) to a different rebar store that has been reclaimed once. Reconverge then overrides local tickets with a foreign store's history.
findings.suggested_fix: When the local epoch is absent, accept supersession only if an independent store identity also matches, such as a stable store id stamped in the record or a shared root ticket-event uuid set. Otherwise keep the DIVERGED refusal. Add this case to `test_unproven_rewrites_keep_the_diverged_refusal`.

Local SNAPSHOT events are derived state') writes new rules for retired-suffix stripping, SNAPSHOT detection and event-file filtering. findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a failure-disposition statement for the override arm: for each step (lineage read, backup ref, reset, replay commit, replay push), state whether a failure is retryable on the next reconverge or fatal, and state that any override failure falls back to the existing DIVERGED refusal with HEAD untouched.
evidence: 'call the override when the remote supersedes; otherwise keep the existing refusal unchanged'
Only two dispositions are stated: 'malformed lineage fails closed like a malformed `epoch`' and the stale-path WARNING. Nothing covers override-step failure or replay-push failure.
findings.finding: The plan turns the DIVERGED refusal into a new override arm but never states the disposition when that arm itself fails. Possible failures include reset --hard, backup-ref creation, replay commit, epoch/lineage read errors on the remote record, and the follow-on push of the replay commit. The plan does not say whether each is retryable (re-attempted on the next reconverge) or fatal (surfaced as DIVERGED or another error that blocks writes). It also does not say which disposition wins when the override fails after the refusal path was bypassed.
findings.location: Scope: `src/rebar/_store/sync.py` ('call the override when the remote supersedes; otherwise keep the existing refusal unchanged')
scenarios: reset --hard fails because the working tree is locked or a file is in use: the plan does not say whether the clone reports DIVERGED, raises, or retries next cycle.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State in the leaf (and record on parent 536b, or in docs/concurrency.md's reconnect paragraph) that 'stale' uses the oldest-unpushed-event ts as its proxy for C3's 'last remote convergence'. Name the inbound-converging/push-failing clone case and say which way it resolves, so the leaf and parent definitions match.
evidence: Leaf: "The clone is *stale* iff its oldest unpushed event's `ts` is older than `now − [reclaim].horizon_days` … Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence."
Parent C3: "any clone whose last remote convergence is older than N days is **forced to reset local `tickets` to remote** on reconnect and may NOT reintroduce E by merge/rebase."
Parent design S3 line: "live clones (< N days) merge normally at swap; staler clones are refused a reintroducing merge and reset to remote (accepted loss)."
ADR 0106 §5 (sibling S0) frames the accepted loss as work the clone 'had ≥ N days … to push', which supports the leaf's proxy, but the parent epic's own C3 wording is about convergence time.
findings.finding: The leaf changes the test for 'stale'. The parent defines a stale clone as one 'whose last remote convergence is older than N days' (C3). The leaf classifies a clone as stale iff its OLDEST UNPUSHED EVENT's ts is older than now − horizon_days, arguing that under I5 auto-push the two are the same. They differ in an edge case the parent's wording covers differently: a clone that keeps fetching and reconverging inbound while its pushes keep failing (e.g. auth or permission rejection) for more than N days. The parent calls that clone fresh (it converged recently) and would replay its unpushed writes. The leaf calls it stale and discards them. The reverse also holds: a clone offline for more than N days whose first unpushed write is recent is stale to the parent but fresh to the leaf, which replays that write. The leaf's uuid-known-to-remote rule still prevents resurrection, so this is a definitional refinement, not a contract break.
findings.location: Approach step 2 'Stale vs fresh' vs parent 536b-8930-b922-4063 DESIGN+PROOF comment C3 and Operator decision ('a clone whose last convergence with the remote is older than N days')
scenarios: A clone fetches daily but its pushes have been rejected for 31 days. After the publish-swap, the parent's definition says fresh (replay), but the leaf discards 31 days of writes and only leaves them on refs/rebar/stale-override/<stamp>.

A clone offline for 40 days writes one event just before reconnecting. The parent's C3 says force-reset; the leaf replays the event. That is harmless (no resurrection), but it does not match the parent's wording.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one sentence to Approach step 2 and to the docs/concurrency.md 'Reconnect after a history reclaim' paragraph: "Staleness is measured by the oldest unpushed local event, a conservative proxy for C3's 'last remote convergence' under I5. A clone that converges inbound but cannot push for more than N days is treated as stale; its work stays recoverable from refs/rebar/stale-override/<stamp>." Then post a matching note on epic 536b so the parent records the refinement (the parent wins on conflicts).

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Base the stale test on a convergence signal (e.g. the commit date of the clone's last-known remote tip before this fetch, or the ADR's merge-base-vs-checkpoint test), or restate the rationale accurately and say explicitly which misclassification direction is accepted and why.
evidence: Plan: 'Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence.'
ADR 0106 §5: 'A clone whose last convergence predates the horizon ("stale") … This is detected by comparing the clone's tickets merge-base against the checkpoint'.
stale_override.py:98 `stale = bool(unpushed) and min(event.ts for event in unpushed) < cutoff` — a single old event decides for the whole clone.
findings.finding: The stale/fresh test is a stand-in for ADR §5's graph-based definition, and the plan's justification is only true in one direction. An unpushed event at time t proves only that the clone has not converged since t. So 'oldest unpushed ts < cutoff' implies stale, but the reverse fails: a clone offline longer than N days that wrote yesterday is classified fresh. Separately, one long-stuck failed push (e.g. a rejected write) on an otherwise always-online clone marks it stale and discards all of its recent work. The plan states 'the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence' as if it decided both cases.
findings.location: Approach step 2 'Stale vs fresh'
scenarios: Clone offline 45 days (horizon 30) writes an EDIT yesterday: classified fresh, so events written against a pre-reclaim view are replayed.
Clone online every day but holding one 40-day-old event whose push was refused: classified stale, so every recent unpushed event is discarded.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Either restate the rule honestly (classify by age of unpushed work and explain why replaying recent uuid-novel events is safe regardless of last-convergence time), or derive last convergence from a recorded signal (e.g. the timestamp of the last successfully fetched/merged remote tip) and classify on that.
evidence: "Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence."
Context: "a clone whose last convergence predates the N-day reclaim horizon OVERRIDE its local `tickets`"
findings.finding: The staleness argument is directionally unsound. If every write auto-pushes, the clone's last convergence happened BEFORE its oldest unpushed write, so the oldest unpushed `ts` is an UPPER bound on last-convergence time, not a lower one. A clone that last converged 100 days ago, sat offline with no writes, and then wrote yesterday is classified 'fresh' and replays, even though by ADR 0106 §5's definition it is stale ('last convergence predates the N-day reclaim horizon'). The Context and the classification rule therefore disagree.
findings.location: Approach step 2 (Stale vs fresh) vs Context/Problem
scenarios: A long-offline clone with only recent local writes replays them on top of a baseline it never converged with. The plan does not state whether this is intended (it is safe given the uuid rule) or a misclassification.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Either show that the oldest unpushed event time is a sound proxy for ADR 0106 §5's 'last convergence' (covering long-offline clones and clones with failing pushes), or record the gap as an explicit deviation/residual in the plan and the ADR.
evidence: Plan: "Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence."
ADR 0106 §5 (lines 116-121): "A clone whose **last convergence predates the horizon** (\"stale\") ... MUST override local with remote".
src/rebar/_store/stale_override.py:98 `stale = bool(unpushed) and min(event.ts for event in unpushed) < cutoff`, where `ts` is the HLC filename prefix and not a convergence timestamp.
Ticket ac32 notes that push failures are only logged and `sync.push=async` sends output to DEVNULL, so long-unpushed-but-converged clones are possible.
findings.finding: The stale-classification premise 'the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence' only holds in one direction. A clone converges, pushes, and then has unpushed writes, so the oldest unpushed write time T and the last convergence time C satisfy T >= C. That makes T an upper bound on C, not an equivalent measure. ADR 0106 §5 defines 'stale' as last convergence predating the horizon. A clone that was offline far longer than N days and wrote only yesterday is stale under the ADR but fresh under the plan. Separately, a clone whose pushes kept failing while fetch/merge succeeded has T < C, so the bound fails in that case too. Nothing in the plan or the code checks either assumption.
findings.location: Approach step 2 (Stale vs fresh)
scenarios: A clone offline for 60 days with N=30 writes one event the day before reconnecting. It is classified fresh and replays, which contradicts the ADR's definition of stale.
A clone whose push fails silently for 40 days while fetch keeps converging. It is classified stale and its recent work is discarded, even though it converged recently.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Document in `docs/concurrency.md` the safe recovery from `refs/rebar/stale-override/*`: re-create individual discarded events as new writes on the reclaimed baseline, never by resetting or merging the backup ref. State the backup refs' retention, and make sure the `rebar store fsck` hint points at that procedure.
evidence: Plan: "logs a WARNING naming the backup ref and the discarded event count — the accepted residual loss". No recovery procedure is given.
sync.py:161-166 failure hint: "the previous tip is kept under refs/rebar/stale-override/* — run: rebar store fsck"
AC 4 lists "lineage proof, stale classification, backup ref, accepted loss" for the docs but no recovery/rollback procedure
Backup refs accumulate one per override (timestamped) and the plan gives no retention policy
findings.finding: The back-out and post-override state are not specified. The plan creates `refs/rebar/stale-override/<stamp>` but never says how an operator recovers from it, how long it is kept, or that simply restoring it is NOT a valid rollback. Pointing `tickets` back at the backup ref re-wedges the clone in DIVERGED, and any manual merge resurrects reclaimed events. The failure-path log tells the operator to run `rebar store fsck`, and the plan never says that fsck/fsck-recover know about these refs.
findings.location: Approach step 3/4; Scope bullet `docs/concurrency.md`; AC 4 (docs evidence)
scenarios: An operator wants a discarded stale event back and runs `git reset --hard refs/rebar/stale-override/…`. The clone goes back to DIVERGED, and a follow-up merge reintroduces pre-collapse history.
A partial-failure warning sends the operator to `rebar store fsck`, which may not look at the backup ref.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the override resumable: build the replay commit (e.g. via index/commit-tree on top of the pinned remote) before moving HEAD, then update HEAD atomically, or record a pending-replay marker that the next reconverge completes; make backup ref names collision-proof; add an interruption test.
evidence: "Point `refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp>` at the old local HEAD ... then `reset --hard` to the pinned remote commit."
"A fresh clone re-adds its unpushed event files ... in ONE local commit on top of the remote"
There is no described recovery, journal or pending-replay marker, and no test for interruption between reset and replay.
findings.finding: The backup → reset → replay sequence is not crash-safe or idempotent. Suppose the process dies (or the replay commit fails) after `reset --hard` but before the replay commit. On the next reconverge, HEAD equals the remote, so a merge-base exists and the override branch never re-runs. The fresh clone's unpushed events then remain only in the backup ref and are silently lost from the store, with no warning. The plan also does not address `<utc-stamp>` collisions if two overrides happen within the same stamp resolution.
findings.location: Approach steps 3–4; Scope `stale_override.py`
scenarios: SIGKILL or a disk-full error during replay of a fresh clone. The user's recent unpushed events vanish from the working store; only a local ref few users know about retains them.
findings.suggested_fix: Construct the replay commit object first by writing the replayed blobs into a tree based on the pinned remote commit and running `commit-tree` with the remote as parent. Then create the backup ref and use a single `reset --hard <replay-commit>` (or `update-ref` + checkout). A crash then leaves either the old HEAD or the final state, never an intermediate one. Suffix backup ref names with a short random or uuid component.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State as an explicit invariant (in the plan and docs/concurrency.md, referenced by S2) that a reclaimed baseline must expose every reclaimed event uuid as a file or in a same-ticket SNAPSHOT `source_event_uuids`, and add a test that a remote missing a ticket's events entirely is handled per that invariant (refuse, or treat as reclaimed).
evidence: "This is the no-resurrection rule: anything the remote folded or retired is known to it and is not re-added."
Tests cover only `.retired` and SNAPSHOT-folded forms. No invariant is stated that S2's swap must preserve uuid visibility for every reclaimed event.
findings.finding: The no-resurrection rule silently depends on an S2 reclaim contract that the plan does not state. Every reclaimed event must remain visible on the remote tip, either as a file (any suffix) or in a SNAPSHOT's `source_event_uuids` for that same ticket. If the publish-swap ever drops events another way (e.g. purging a whole ticket directory, or folding without listing uuids), a fresh clone will treat those pushed-and-reclaimed events as 'unpushed' and replay them. That is the resurrection the horizon exists to prevent.
findings.location: Approach step 1 (Local-only events); Testing 'No resurrection' bullet
scenarios: S2 implements reclamation of fully closed or archived tickets by deleting their directory. A clone that converged yesterday replays the whole deleted history on reconnect.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the rollout precondition (S2's swap must not run until all clones carry this version, or S2 must check a minimum compat version) and document whether old writers can strip `epoch_lineage`; if they can, raise the compat record version so older clients refuse rather than rewrite.
evidence: "`write_compat_record` ... preserves `epoch_lineage` just as it already preserves `epoch`" applies only to new code.
There is no statement that S2 must gate on clients running this version, and no analysis of pre-lineage writers.
findings.finding: Deploy ordering and old/new coexistence are unspecified. This behavior only helps clones that already run this version when S2's publish-swap executes. The plan also does not state what happens if an older client rewrites `.store-compat.json` without knowing about `epoch_lineage` and pushes it, which could strip the lineage proof for every other clone.
findings.location: Approach (compat.py paragraph); Context ('S2 publish-swap ... can rely on')
scenarios: A pre-upgrade clone re-stamps the compat record after the swap. Newer clones then see no lineage and wedge in DIVERGED, which is the very failure this story fixes.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the fresh-clone override atomic and idempotent: build the replay commit on top of the pinned remote before moving HEAD, then move HEAD in one ref update; add a test that interrupts between steps and verifies retry recovery.
evidence: 'Point `refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp>` at the old local HEAD (local only, never pushed), then `reset --hard` to the pinned remote commit.'
'A fresh clone re-adds its unpushed event files byte-identically … in ONE local commit on top of the remote'
The Testing section has no interrupted-override or retry case.
findings.finding: The override is a multi-step, non-atomic mutation: update backup ref, then reset --hard, then build the replay commit. A retry cannot recover it. If the process dies or the commit fails after the reset but before the replay commit, HEAD already equals the remote. The next reconverge then finds a shared merge-base, never re-enters stale_override, and the fresh clone's unpushed events survive only in the local-only backup ref. That is silent loss of writes the plan promises to keep.

The codebase does not guarantee this. When a ticket is compacted again, the new SNAPSHOT's `source_event_uuids` lists only the live candidates; it never lists the earlier SNAPSHOT or that SNAPSHOT's sources. So once an older SNAPSHOT and its `.retired` sources leave the tree, the remote has no record of those uuids. findings.finding: The override is not atomic and cannot resume. Step 3 resets to the remote first, and only then does step 4 build a separate replay commit for a fresh clone. If the replay fails (update-index, checkout or commit error, or the process dies) after the reset, HEAD already equals the remote. On the next reconverge, HEAD and the remote share a merge-base, so the unrelated-history branch, and with it the override and replay, never runs again. The fresh clone's unpushed in-horizon events are left only in the backup ref with no further warning. That is exactly the loss the fresh/stale split exists to prevent. findings.suggested_fix: Add a short 'Prior art' note under Approach. Git's own advice for an upstream rewrite is to rebase local work onto the new upstream and skip changes it already has.
